power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: • Early adversity biases precision in specific channels, not as a global gain.
• Precision-only and maladaptive-prior accounts make dissociable predictions.
• Sensitive-period brakes and self-confirming sampling can stabilize calibration.
• The ACC is proposed as a hub within a distributed precision circuit.
• Supportive input predicts faster precision re-tuning, not a mirror image of harm.
>Introduction: The Predicting Brain and the Developing Brain
text.formatted: <head n="1." >Introduction: The Predicting Brain and the Developing Brain</head>

text.text: One increasingly influential perspective in cognitive neuroscience conceptualizes the brain not as a passive, stimulus-driven processor of external information, but as a proactive, hypothesis-testing organ that continuously generates and updates predictions about the world (Clark, 2013; Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: One increasingly influential perspective in cognitive neuroscience conceptualizes the brain not as a passive, stimulus-driven processor of external information, but as a proactive, hypothesis-testing organ that continuously generates and updates predictions about the world <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Clark, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: This view is most formally articulated within predictive coding and predictive processing frameworks, which have been applied to perception, action, cognition, and psychopathology (Hohwy, 2013; Rao and Ballard, 1999).
text.formatted: This view is most formally articulated within predictive coding and predictive processing frameworks, which have been applied to perception, action, cognition, and psychopathology <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Hohwy, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">Rao and Ballard, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: These frameworks are neither new nor uncontested (Section 3.3), and they should not be treated as universally applicable explanatory models.

Rather, they provide an integrative lens through which specific developmental processes may be re-examined, including how early experiences shape expectations, regulatory systems, and adaptive responses to environmental demands.

We use predictive processing (PP) as the general term for this family of theories, and reserve predictive coding for the specific hierarchical, message-passing implementation in which each cortical level predicts the activity of the level below and forwards only the residual prediction error (Rao and Ballard, 1999).
text.formatted: We use predictive processing (PP) as the general term for this family of theories, and reserve predictive coding for the specific hierarchical, message-passing implementation in which each cortical level predicts the activity of the level below and forwards only the residual prediction error <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Rao and Ballard, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: At its core, PP holds that the brain constructs and continuously refines a generative model of the world to infer the causes of its sensory input, minimizing prediction error, the discrepancy between what is predicted and what is sensed (Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: At its core, PP holds that the brain constructs and continuously refines a generative model of the world to infer the causes of its sensory input, minimizing prediction error, the discrepancy between what is predicted and what is sensed <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Perception is then not a bottom-up reconstruction of reality from raw sense data, but a model-driven process in which sensory input primarily serves to correct predictions (Clark, 2013).
text.formatted: Perception is then not a bottom-up reconstruction of reality from raw sense data, but a model-driven process in which sensory input primarily serves to correct predictions <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Clark, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: If the brain is a prediction machine, its foundational models are not fixed at birth but are calibrated by experience.

Early life, particularly the period from conception to two years of age, is marked by unparalleled neuroplasticity, during which environmental exposures shape emerging structural and functional architecture (Van den Bergh et al., 2020; Van den Bergh et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Early life, particularly the period from conception to two years of age, is marked by unparalleled neuroplasticity, during which environmental exposures shape emerging structural and functional architecture <ref type="bibr" target="#b141">(Van den Bergh et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Van den Bergh et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This plasticity is not uniform in time: it is organized into critical and sensitive periods that open and close on different schedules in different neural systems, and whose closure is actively regulated (Hensch, 2005; Knudsen, 2004).
text.formatted: This plasticity is not uniform in time: it is organized into critical and sensitive periods that open and close on different schedules in different neural systems, and whose closure is actively regulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Hensch, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Knudsen, 2004)</ref>.

text.text: From a dynamicsystems perspective, development is an emergent property of the reciprocal coupling of organism and environment; early caregiver-infant interactions establish stable yet flexible "attractor states" that canalize long-term trajectories (Montirosso et al., 2020; Provenzi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: From a dynamicsystems perspective, development is an emergent property of the reciprocal coupling of organism and environment; early caregiver-infant interactions establish stable yet flexible "attractor states" that canalize long-term trajectories <ref type="bibr" target="#b97">(Montirosso et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b113">Provenzi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: The statistical regularities, affective tone, and predictability of the early environment provide the foundational "training data" for the brain's generative models.

Calibration is not limited to adversity: the developing brain is experience-expectant and depends on structured, supportive input to organize adaptively (Greenough et al., 1987; Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020).
text.formatted: Calibration is not limited to adversity: the developing brain is experience-expectant and depends on structured, supportive input to organize adaptively <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Greenough et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Section 2 sets out these developmental foundations before the computational account is introduced, because they determine why early calibration matters disproportionately and why it can persist.

This article bridges PP and developmental psychopathology by proposing a framework for the lasting impact of ELA, a broad construct spanning prenatal stress and perinatal complications through neglectful or abusive caregiving (Chertoff et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This article bridges PP and developmental psychopathology by proposing a framework for the lasting impact of ELA, a broad construct spanning prenatal stress and perinatal complications through neglectful or abusive caregiving <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Chertoff et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Although our title concerns adversity, we treat ELA as one pole of a broader early-life environment that ranges from depriving to supportive, because the same predictive machinery is calibrated across this whole range.
We argue that ELA does not simply inflict increased risk; it calibrates a predictive architecture toward survival in an environment experienced as hostile, unpredictable, or unsupportive.
The framework makes two claims of graded strength: 1.
Core (parsimonious) claim: altered precision weighting.

ELA primarily recalibrates how much each prediction error counts: assigning high precision (gain) to potentialthreat signals and to predictable input that would normally be attenuated, while assigning low precision to evidence that disconfirms expectations of threat or signals benign novelty.
This claim requires no commitment to the content of highlevel beliefs.
Stronger (optional) claim: maladaptive priors.
Under sustained adversity, these precision biases can become entrenched as rigid, pessimistic content priors about the self, others, and the world.
This claim is more explanatorily ambitious and correspondingly more demanding empirically, because it attributes specific belief content to the developing system.

PP accounts have been applied to psychopathology and, in particular, to autism, where atypical precision has been proposed as a core computational feature (Lawson et al., 2014; Van de Cruys et al., 2014).
text.formatted: PP accounts have been applied to psychopathology and, in particular, to autism, where atypical precision has been proposed as a core computational feature <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">(Lawson et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b136">Van de Cruys et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: What we add is fourfold.

First, we argue that ELA-related precision dysregulation is channel-specific and biased rather than global, and we commit to this specificity in an explicit mapping from dimensions of early experience to predicted precision channels (Section 4.4, Table 2).

text.text: Second, we specify behavioral, computational, and neural signatures that would distinguish altered precision from altered priors (Section 4.3, Table 1).
text.formatted: Second, we specify behavioral, computational, and neural signatures that would distinguish altered precision from altered priors (Section 4.3, Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">1</ref>).

text.text: Third, we anchor the calibration in developmental mechanisms (sensitive periods, plasticity brakes, and individual differences in susceptibility; Section 2) and in a distributed circuit in which the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) is proposed as a hub for allocating gain across channels (Section 5).
Fourth, we hold the account to a symmetry constraint, in which the same machinery is calibrated by supportive as well as adverse input, with an asymmetric prediction of its own (Section 7.2).
Two scope statements frame what follows.

The framework's primary domain is threat vigilance and affective learning and decision-making under uncertainty; extensions to other outcomes are secondary and are flagged as such, and Section 7.3 states the processes the framework does not claim to explain.
Its evidential basis is the published literature reviewed here.

Prenatal-anxiety findings from two longitudinal cohorts, published individually and synthesized through the present lens in a companion paper (Van den Bergh and Frasch, 2026), are used as illustrations of compatibility, not as independent tests, because the same findings partly motivated the framework.
>Developmental Foundations: Why Early Calibration Matters and Why It Persists
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Developmental Foundations: Why Early Calibration Matters and Why It Persists</head>

text.text: The influence of experience on the developing brain is not constant over time but concentrated in windows of heightened plasticity.

In a critical period, a circuit needs a specific, species-typical input to develop typically, and missing that input has lasting consequences; a sensitive period is a wider window in which experience shapes development strongly but does not dictate it (Gabard-Durnam and McLaughlin, 2020; Knudsen, 2004; Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020). Greenough et al. (1987) linked such windows to two kinds of plasticity.

(1987)</ref> linked such windows to two kinds of plasticity.

text.text: Experience-expectant plasticity relies on input that every member of the species can count on, such as patterned sensory stimulation and contingent social interaction, and for which the brain is prepared in advance.

Experiencedependent plasticity stores what is particular to an individual's environment: how sensitive the caregiving is, and how much threat, deprivation, or unpredictability the child meets (Chertoff et al., 2026; Teicher and Samson, 2016).
text.formatted: Experiencedependent plasticity stores what is particular to an individual's environment: how sensitive the caregiving is, and how much threat, deprivation, or unpredictability the child meets <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Chertoff et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b132">Teicher and Samson, 2016)</ref>.

text.text: This distinction matters for the present account.
An input counts as experience-expectant only if the brain is prepared for it as a normal part of development, and most forms of adversity fail this test.

Adversity therefore acts mainly as an experience-dependent input to calibration rather than as an expected signal shaping circuits through canonical criticalperiod mechanisms (Chertoff et al., 2026; Gabard-Durnam and McLaughlin, 2020).
text.formatted: Adversity therefore acts mainly as an experience-dependent input to calibration rather than as an expected signal shaping circuits through canonical criticalperiod mechanisms <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Chertoff et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Gabard-Durnam and McLaughlin, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Deprivation is the partial exception: it is the absence of expected input, a violation of the expectable environment (Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020), and we accordingly predict a different precision profile for deprivation than for threat (Table 2).
text.formatted: Deprivation is the partial exception: it is the absence of expected input, a violation of the expectable environment <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020</ref>), and we accordingly predict a different precision profile for deprivation than for threat (Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">2</ref>).

text.text: In PP terms, experienceexpectant input supplies the structured statistics from which usable generative models and adaptive precision estimates are built; experience-dependent input tunes those estimates to the particular statistics of an individual's environment.

Windows differ between systems: sensory systems have early windows, whereas amygdala-prefrontal circuitry, the ACC, and association cortex mature later and remain plastic into adolescence, a second sensitive period for threat, reward, and control (Chertoff et al., 2026; Gee et al., 2013; Larsen and Luna, 2018).

text.text: Prenatally, maternal signals reach the fetus through biological channels (maternal cortisol and placental corticotropin-releasing hormone, maternal heart rate and circadian rhythms, uterine blood flow, and maternal movement and voice), and fetal responses to changes in maternal psychophysiological state are measurable from mid-gestation (DiPietro et al., 2008; Van den Bergh et al., 2020).

text.text: Timing within gestation also matters: in the Leuven cohort, maternal anxiety at 12 to 22 weeks of gestation, rather than later in pregnancy, was associated with impulsivity and poorer endogenous cognitive control in adolescence (Mennes et al., 2006; Van den Bergh et al., 2005), a period of intense neuronal migration and early cortical organization.

text.text: We therefore expect different precision channels to be calibrated in different windows, a commitment made explicit in the window column of Table 2.

text.text: The opening and closure of plasticity windows are regulated by identifiable mechanisms: the maturation of parvalbumin-positive inhibitory interneurons and the resulting excitation-inhibition balance, the formation of perineuronal nets that stabilize synapses, and epigenetic and neuro-glial "brakes" that restrict later remodeling (Hensch, 2005; Takesian and Hensch, 2013; see Chertoff et al., 2026, for a review).

text.text: Two observations link these gates directly to precision.

First, the neuromodulators proposed to set precision (Section 5.4) also gate developmental plasticity: catecholamine depletion prevents experience-dependent ocular-dominance plasticity during the visual critical period (Kasamatsu and Pettigrew, 1976), and the cholinergic brake Lynx1 limits plasticity in adult cortex (Morishita et al., 2010).

text.text: Second, adversity can shift window timing.

Early stress has been associated with accelerated maturation of amygdala-prefrontal connectivity in previously institutionalized children (Gee et al., 2013; see Callaghan and Tottenham, 2016, for the stress-acceleration hypothesis), environmental factors influence the pace of brain development more generally (Tooley et al., 2021), and in mice early-life stress induces precocious critical-period timing with premature perineuronal-net formation (Poplawski et al., 2024).

text.text: Together these findings suggest a specific developmental hypothesis: precision set-points are learned from the statistics of the environment while the relevant window is open, under the control of neuromodulatory systems that are themselves gates on plasticity, and are stabilized when the brakes engage.
If adversity also accelerates closure, the set-point would be fixed earlier, from a shorter and more adverse sample of experience, and with less opportunity for later correction.
Experience becomes biologically embedded through lasting molecular and physiological changes (Berens et al., 2017; Lupien et al., 2009).

text.text: ELA alters DNA methylation of stressregulatory genes such as the glucocorticoid receptor gene NR3C1, a molecular memory of the early environment (Berens et al., 2017), and can recalibrate the hypothalamic-pituitaryadrenal (HPA) axis toward hyper-responsive or blunted reactivity, with consequences for glucocorticoid-receptor-dense regions such as the hippocampus, amygdala, and prefrontal cortex (Lupien et al., 2009; McEwen, 2012).

text.text: Prenatally, embedding begins in utero: maternal stress signals reach the fetus through the maternal-placental-fetal interface, where placental regulation, for example of the glucocorticoid-inactivating enzyme 11β-HSD2, partly determines fetal exposure (Van den Bergh et al., 2020).

text.text: We speak of developmental "signs" rather than only "scars": the same machinery embeds supportive caregiving, whose marks are as durable but adaptive (Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020; Van den Bergh et al., 2024).
text.formatted: We speak of developmental "signs" rather than only "scars": the same machinery embeds supportive caregiving, whose marks are as durable but adaptive <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">(Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b138">Van den Bergh et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Plasticity explains why early experience can change neural function; it does not by itself explain why an adaptation persists after the conditions that elicited it have changed.
We propose three complementary mechanisms, the third of which is specific to the predictive account.
Structural stabilization.
Once plasticity brakes engage (Section 2.2), set-points learned during the window become harder to revise, so a calibration acquired early is carried forward by circuit structure.
Molecular and physiological memory.
Epigenetic marks and recalibrated HPA setpoints (Section 2.3) maintain an altered internal milieu that continues to bias neuromodulatory tone, and hence precision, in later life.
A system that assigns low precision to disconfirming evidence discounts exactly the evidence that would retune it.
Under active inference, it also selects actions, such as avoidance and reduced exploration, that make such evidence less likely to be sampled at all (Friston, 2010; Lloyd et al., 2022).

text.text: The calibration thereby protects itself: the information needed to revise it is either down-weighted or never collected.

text.text: >The Architecture of Prediction: A Primer on Predictive Processing
text.formatted: <head n="3." >The Architecture of Prediction: A Primer on Predictive Processing</head>

text.text: The brain does not perceive the world directly; it constructs an internal generative model to infer the hidden causes of sensory signals (Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: The brain does not perceive the world directly; it constructs an internal generative model to infer the hidden causes of sensory signals <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Two terms are often used interchangeably and should be kept apart.

The generative model is the full causal model: its structure (which hidden states exist and how they cause one another and the sensory input), the likelihood mapping from states to signals, and the expectations over states.
A prior is a narrower object, the expectation over a particular hidden state at a particular level before new evidence arrives, for example that light comes from above, or that danger is imminent.

A child can therefore hold an accurate, well-structured generative model of a caregiving environment and still differ from other children in specific priors within it, or in the precision assigned to particular signals.

Higher-level social expectations shaped by repeated caregiving experiences resemble what attachment theory describes as internal working models of self, others, and relationships (Bowlby, 1982; Bretherton, 1992; Tottenham and Vannucci, 2025).
text.formatted: Higher-level social expectations shaped by repeated caregiving experiences resemble what attachment theory describes as internal working models of self, others, and relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Bowlby, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Bretherton, 1992;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b134">Tottenham and Vannucci, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The generative model issues top-down predictions that cascade down the hierarchy (Rao and Ballard, 1999).
text.formatted: The generative model issues top-down predictions that cascade down the hierarchy <ref type="bibr" target="#b115">(Rao and Ballard, 1999)</ref>.

text.text: Predictions are compared with bottom-up input; their discrepancy, the prediction error, is propagated upward, and the system minimizes prediction error by updating the model.
Because only unpredicted input is passed forward, this is an efficient coding scheme (Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: Because only unpredicted input is passed forward, this is an efficient coding scheme <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Not all prediction errors are treated equally; their influence on belief updating is scaled by their precision, the brain's estimate of their reliability (formally, the inverse variance) (Feldman and Friston, 2010).
text.formatted: Not all prediction errors are treated equally; their influence on belief updating is scaled by their precision, the brain's estimate of their reliability (formally, the inverse variance) <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Feldman and Friston, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Precision acts as a gain control on prediction-error units: a precise error drives rapid updating, whereas an imprecise error is discounted and existing beliefs are preserved.
This gain control is widely regarded as a mechanism of attention (Feldman and Friston, 2010), and it lets the brain balance reliance on priors against updating from new evidence.
text.formatted: This gain control is widely regarded as a mechanism of attention <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Feldman and Friston, 2010)</ref>, and it lets the brain balance reliance on priors against updating from new evidence.

text.text: One point of formal discipline should be stated at the outset: precision is not categorically separate from belief, because precision estimates are themselves beliefs about the reliability of signals.
The distinction maintained throughout is between content priors (expectations about latent causes and outcomes) and precision expectations (estimates of the reliability of evidence and predictions).
Precision weighting is the pivot of our framework: it is the component we argue is most directly recalibrated by early adversity.

Low levels of the hierarchy predict simple sensory features; higher levels predict increasingly abstract regularities such as object identities, event sequences, social intentions, and the self (Hohwy, 2013).
text.formatted: Low levels of the hierarchy predict simple sensory features; higher levels predict increasingly abstract regularities such as object identities, event sequences, social intentions, and the self <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">(Hohwy, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Under active inference, action is integrated into the predictive cycle: motor commands are predictions about the sensory consequences of movement, and the body moves to fulfill them (Friston, 2010; Seth and Friston, 2016).

text.text: Action thus also determines which evidence is sampled, which is why avoidance can maintain a calibration (Section 2.4).
Despite its reach, PP faces serious critiques, the most consequential being potential unfalsifiability (Bowman et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Despite its reach, PP faces serious critiques, the most consequential being potential unfalsifiability <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Bowman et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Because the content of priors and the settings of precision are not directly observable, a PP model can often be tuned post hoc to explain almost any outcome (Bowman et al., 2023; Kwisthout et al., 2017).

text.text: Many applications operate in an "as-if" mode, borrowing the mathematics of Bayesian inference to describe behavior without committing to biological implementation (Hodson et al., 2024; Mangalam, 2025).

text.text: The empirical status of the framework's core claims is mixed, and the distinction between them matters here.
The general claims that the brain is sensitive to prediction and that expectation modulates neural responses are well supported.

The specific architectural commitments of predictive coding, distinct prediction and prediction-error units with precision implemented as their gain, have more modest support (Hodson et al., 2024; Walsh et al., 2020).

text.text: PP is better supported as a computational-level account of learning and inference under uncertainty, where modelbased studies estimate precision-like parameters such as learning rates and volatility (Behrens et al., 2007; Mathys et al., 2014), than as a settled account of cortical microcircuitry.

text.text: Our framework is built to rest on the better-supported level: its central constructs (channel-specific precision, volatility-dependent learning rates, prediction-error gain) are estimable from behavior with hierarchical Bayesian models, and its neural claims are stated as hypotheses.
Grounding PP in ELA research also narrows the falsifiability problem, which bites hardest when priors and precision are free parameters of an adult brain considered without its history.
The ELA literature supplies measurable developmental conditions, with documented associations with, and in animal, quasiexperimental, and intervention designs causal influence on, neurodevelopment.

This does not vindicate PP; it constrains otherwise free parameters, which allows the framework to commit to the discriminating predictions of Section 4.3, the channel mapping of Section 4.4, and the boundary conditions of Section 7.3.

text.text: ELA disrupts the capacity to allocate precision flexibly and adaptively.
We distinguish two facets: • Over-precision of potential-threat and predictable input (hypervigilance).

Having "learned" that the environment is dangerous or hard to predict, the system assigns high precision to any signal that might indicate threat, and fails to attenuate precision for repetitive, predictable input that should become irrelevant.
Threataligned prediction errors are amplified, capturing attention and driving updating in a self-reinforcing loop (Adams et al., 2013; Sterzer et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Threataligned prediction errors are amplified, capturing attention and driving updating in a self-reinforcing loop <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adams et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">Sterzer et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: • Under-precision of disconfirming or positive evidence (inflexible updating).
The system assigns low precision to prediction errors that would contradict a threatbiased model; unexpected positive events (kindness, success, safety) are treated as noise (Sterzer et al., 2018).
text.formatted: The system assigns low precision to prediction errors that would contradict a threatbiased model; unexpected positive events (kindness, success, safety) are treated as noise <ref type="bibr" target="#b128">(Sterzer et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: A finding that appears to contradict the hypervigilance profile sharpens it.

Model-based fMRI in a birth cohort followed to adulthood links ELA to reduced expected-value and reward-prediction-error signaling in striatum, ventromedial prefrontal cortex (vmPFC), and ACC (Sacu et al., 2024), and adults with more adverse childhood experiences explore less and underweight recent reward feedback in a foraging task (Lloyd et al., 2022).

text.text: Adolescents exposed to early stress likewise learn stimulus-outcome contingencies more slowly and update them less well after a reversal (Harms et al., 2018).

text.text: The evidence is not one-sided: in a probabilistic learning task, maltreated adolescents showed not only greater choice variability but also biased beliefs about the likelihood of reward (Hanson et al., 2017), a priors-type effect, which indicates that the two mechanisms distinguished in Section 4.3 can co-occur.

text.text: Reduced reward-prediction-error encoding is not what a globally hyper-responsive system would show.

We therefore make the reconciliation explicit: under a limited precision budget, chronic over-weighting of threat-aligned channels is purchased at the cost of under-weighting reward-and value-related channels.
ELA neither raises nor lowers responsiveness globally; it reallocates gain across channels.

This is a testable commitment: within individuals, threat-channel gain and reward-channel encoding should be inversely related, and interventions that reduce threat-channel gain should partially restore reward-prediction-error encoding.
A globally elevated or globally blunted gain profile in the same individuals would count against it.
This dual bias is a form of maladaptive meta-learning: the system has learned a biased rule for how to learn from future evidence (Nussenbaum and Hartley, 2024).

text.text: Precision in this sense is signal-and level-specific, not one global parameter: sensory precision for repeated input, affective-salience precision for threat-related cues, attentional precision for neutral or ambiguous stimuli, and interoceptive precision for bodily signals.
The ELA profile we propose is biased toward particular signals rather than globally elevated, which distinguishes it from the global over-weighting proposed for autism (Section 7.1).

Under sustained adversity, precision biases may consolidate into rigid, pessimistic content priors: exteroceptive priors (social interactions predicted as rejecting; ambiguity predicted to resolve negatively), interoceptive priors (a baseline expectation of high arousal and distress; Barrett et al., 2016), and priors about the self (ineffective, unworthy, or culpable, particularly where a child infers their own inadequacy as the cause of a caregiver's behavior).

text.text: A high-confidence prior resists updating and can manufacture confirming evidence: a person who strongly predicts rejection may perceive a neutral expression as scornful.

Physically abused children, for example, show broadened perceptual categories for anger (Pollak and Kistler, 2002), a finding that could reflect either a shifted prior or altered precision on ambiguous facial cues, and is therefore exactly the kind of result the tests in Section 4.3 are designed to adjudicate.

text.text: We flag explicitly that the priors claim is the framework's strong form.

Published ERP studies of infants and children prenatally exposed to maternal anxiety report enhanced processing of repeated standard tones (van den Heuvel et al., 2015), of fearful relative to happy vocalizations (Otte et al., 2015), and of neutral relative to valenced pictures (van den Heuvel et al., 2018), and related work reports altered auditory and attentional responses after prenatal anxiety or depression (De Asis-Cruz et al., 2020; Harvison et al., 2009; Hennessey et al., 2024; Hunter et al., 2012; Luotonen et al., 2022; Maria et al., 2020).

text.text: Behaviorally, a child with high precision on threat and low precision on safety and a child with pessimistic priors about safety will both show threat-biased decisions.
The two accounts are nonetheless distinguishable, because they locate the bias in different terms of the belief update.
In a simple Gaussian update, the change in a belief μ after a prediction error δ is Δμ = [πδ / (πδ + πμ)] δ, where πδ is the precision of the evidence and πμ the precision of the current belief.

The precision-only account places the ELA effect in π δ , separately for particular channels and for evidence of particular valence; the priors account places it in the starting value of μ (and, in its rigid form, in a high πμ).

These locations make different quantitative predictions, which are summarized in Table 1 and can be estimated trial by trial with hierarchical Bayesian or reinforcement-learning models (Mathys et al., 2011 (Mathys et al., , 2014)).

text.text: The last row answers a question central to any clinical use of the framework.

Under the precision-only account, retuning precision should improve inference even in a person whose early expectations were negative, because those expectations are continuously reestimated from evidence once evidence is weighted appropriately.
Under the priors account, retuning precision leaves pessimistic beliefs intact until enough disconfirming evidence has accumulated.

Existing findings are suggestive but not decisive: reduced value and reward-prediction-error signaling (Sacu et al., 2024) and underweighting of reward feedback (Lloyd et al., 2022) are effects on evidence weighting, as the precision account predicts, whereas biased beliefs about reward likelihood in maltreated adolescents (Hanson et al., 2017) are a priors-type effect; none of these studies compared the two accounts on the same data.

text.text: The prenatal-anxiety literature supplies a second illustration from adolescence and adulthood.

Neither illustration was designed as a test; the decisive studies would fit both accounts to the same trial-by-trial data.
A falsifiable framework must also state which dimensions of early experience bias which channels, in which direction.

Treating "ELA" as one exposure would purchase explanatory coverage at the price of falsifiability, because prenatal maternal anxiety, physical threat, deprivation, environmental unpredictability, and rigidly invariant input differ in timing, severity, controllability, sensory statistics, and social content.

Dimensional models distinguish threat from deprivation as separable exposures with distinct neurodevelopmental consequences (McLaughlin et al., 2020; Sheridan and McLaughlin, 2014), and the unpredictability of parental and environmental signals has emerged as a third, separable calibrator of developing circuits (Davis and Glynn, 2024; Glynn and Baram, 2019).

text.text: Precision dysregulation is unlikely to reside in one region.
We propose that it is implemented by a distributed circuit and that the ACC is a hub within it, and we separate two claims that differ in evidential strength.

The first, well supported, is that the ACC performs computations central to precision: it tracks surprise and volatility, signals errors, and computes the expected value of control (Behrens et al., 2007; Shenhav et al., 2013).

text.text: The second, more specific and so far untested, is that ELA-related alterations of the ACC mediate the precision changes proposed here.

Developmental evidence that ACC structure and function are altered after adversity exists (Cohen et al., 2006; Sacu et al., 2024; Teicher and Samson, 2016), but mediation has not been demonstrated, and it is stated below as a hypothesis with a test.

text.text: We privilege the ACC for three reasons.

It integrates the variables that a gain-allocation decision requires (volatility, value, and the cost of control) (Behrens et al., 2007; Shenhav et al., 2013); together with the orbitofrontal cortex (OFC) it provides prominent top-down input to the locus coeruleus, an anatomical route by which cortical estimates of uncertainty and value can set noradrenergic gain (Aston-Jones and Cohen, 2005); and it matures late, giving it a long window for calibration (Section 2.1).

text.text: Its divisions also differ: the dorsal ACC and anterior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) track volatility, surprise, and the expected value of control, whereas subgenual and perigenual divisions, with the vmPFC, track affective value and autonomic outflow.
Sections 5.1 and 5.2 concern primarily the dorsal division, and predictions for the two should not be interchanged.
The dorsal ACC (dACC) responds robustly to errors, whether detected internally or signaled by negative feedback (Holroyd et al., 2004), positioning it to compute and broadcast prediction errors.

text.text: Its activity tracks trial-by-trial Bayesian surprise (unsigned prediction error) independently of valence, implicating it in detecting volatility and signaling when the generative model is failing (Behrens et al., 2007; Hayden et al., 2011).

text.text: ACC error signals are modulated by value: single neurons in primates fire more strongly when a larger predicted reward is lost (Amiez et al., 2006; Kennerley et al., 2006), and the dACC integrates reward over longer timescales, providing a filtered history of outcomes needed to update value-based expectations (Seo and Lee, 2007).

text.text: We hypothesize biased ACC gain allocation rather than global hyper-responsiveness: chronic early stress and unpredictability re-allocate the ACC's limited gain toward unsigned surprise and threat-aligned error signaling, and away from signed reward prediction errors and expected value.

A persistently amplified surprise signal, reporting that the world model is inadequate even in safe contexts, could drive rumination; the same reallocation predicts the reduced expected-value and reward-prediction-error encoding in ACC, vmPFC, and striatum observed after ELA (Sacu et al., 2024).

text.text: The claim requires distinguishing what a bare "hyper-responsive ACC" conflates (signed versus unsigned errors, threat versus reward domains, task-evoked reactivity versus model-derived parameters, tonic versus phasic activity, developmental stage), and it is falsified by uniformly elevated or uniformly blunted ACC responses across these dimensions in the same individuals.

Mediation can be tested longitudinally, by measuring early exposure, later ACC volatility and gain-allocation signals, and later precision parameters in the same individuals, and causally, by manipulating ACC activity in animal models during and after the relevant window.
The ACC is one node, and several others make contributions it does not.

text.text: This decomposition makes the ACC hypothesis falsifiable at the circuit level.

If ELA-related biases are confined to threat cues and are independent of volatility, an amygdala-based account fits better; if they are specific to bodily signals, an insula-based account fits better; if they appear only when task states are hidden, the OFC is implicated in the content of the model rather than in gain.
The ACC hypothesis predicts a bias that spans stimulus classes, scales with volatility and control demands, and shows the inverse threat-reward relation of Section 4.1.

Precision weighting, gain control on prediction-error units, is widely proposed to be set by noradrenaline from the locus coeruleus (LC-NE) and acetylcholine from the basal forebrain (Feldman and Friston, 2010).

text.text: A computational division of labor has been proposed in which acetylcholine signals expected uncertainty and noradrenaline unexpected uncertainty (Yu and Dayan, 2005), and human pharmacology supports distinct roles: noradrenergic antagonism alters learning about unexpected changes, cholinergic antagonism alters the attribution of uncertainty to chance versus contextual change (Marshall et al., 2016), and the β-adrenergic antagonist propranolol reduces learning rates and the influence of volatility on belief updating and pupil-linked arousal (Lawson et al., 2021).

text.text: We therefore propose a concrete chain: ELA alters LC-NE and basal-forebrain cholinergic development, which biases precision set-points while plasticity windows are open, producing the hypervigilant, poorly attenuating phenotype of Section 4.1.
To our knowledge, developmental neurochemistry has not yet been tied to computational precision estimates in ELA cohorts, which is itself a testable gap.
Dopamine requires separate treatment, because dopaminergic signaling and precision weighting are distinct constructs that interact.
Phasic dopamine activity encodes reward prediction errors (Schultz et al., 1997), a signal that precision then scales.

text.text: Dopamine thus enters the framework at two points: as a generator of the reward-prediction-error signals whose gain we propose ELA reallocates, and as a candidate substrate of policy precision, which governs exploration and avoidance.
Early adversity alters mesocorticolimbic dopamine in ways that fit the gain-reallocation claim.

In humans, low reported early parental care was associated with greater stressinduced ventral striatal dopamine release in a small PET study (Pruessner et al., 2004), childhood adversity has been associated with greater amphetamine-induced ventral striatal dopamine release (Oswald et al., 2014) and with elevated presynaptic striatal dopamine function in young adulthood (Egerton et al., 2016), and emotional neglect predicts blunted ventral striatal development in adolescence (Hanson et al., 2015; see Novick et al., 2018, for a review of reward processing after early stress).

text.text: Read together, these findings suggest sensitized dopaminergic responses to stress and threat alongside blunted reward-related responses, the dopaminergic counterpart of the reallocation in Section 4.1, rather than a uniform increase or decrease.
Two predictions follow.

Computationally, ELA should lower policy precision for rewardseeking actions, reducing exploration and favoring avoidance (consistent with Lloyd et al., 2022), a parameter separable from perceptual learning rates (Table 3).

text.text: Causally, the animal manipulations above can be combined with computational phenotyping: juvenile Otx2 knockdown in the ventral tegmental area, or partial silencing of amygdala corticotropin-releasing hormone, should shift learning-rate asymmetries and exploration parameters in probabilistic reversal and foraging tasks in the predicted directions, and their reversal should normalize them.

text.text: The "model-error" and "model-precision" labels used below are interpretive constructions of this framework, not established identities of the gradients.
• The "model-error" gradient (G1): a hierarchy from transmodal association cortex (e.g., the default mode network, DMN) to unimodal sensory and motor cortex.

Its transmodal apex corresponds to regions initiating abstract top-down predictions, its unimodal end to regions processing bottom-up input and generating prediction errors (Huntenburg et al., 2018; Margulies et al., 2016).

text.text: We hypothesize that ELA perturbs the normative development of these gradients, because a brain adapting to chronic threat must prioritize reactive sensory monitoring over abstract, long-range prediction.

ELA may compress the model-error gradient, operationalized as reduced G1 range and dispersion, reduced eccentricity of transmodal regions, reduced alignment with a normative template, and delayed developmental expansion, each computable and anchored in documented normative maturation of cortical gradients (Dong et al., 2021; Paquola et al., 2019).

text.text: The framework supports a transdiagnostic reframing stated in terms of precision first; the profiles below differ in which signals are over-or under-weighted, and the ELA profile we propose is the biased, threat-confirming variant.
• Depression: over-precise negative expectations about self, world, and future, such that positive prediction errors are assigned low precision and ignored (Badcock et al., 2017; Kube et al., 2020).

text.text: • Anxiety disorders: chronically high uncertainty with imprecise priors about safety, compensated by up-regulated precision on bottom-up prediction errors, yielding hypervigilance, arousal, and worry (Adams et al., 2013; Sterzer et al., 2018).

text.text: • Behavioral and computational: in probabilistic-learning tasks, individuals with ELA histories should show faster learning from negative and slower learning from positive feedback, with the asymmetry persisting in stable environments (precision account) rather than decaying from a shifted baseline (priors account).
A priorsspecific signature would be valenced bias in baseline expectations before evidence arrives.
• Neuroimaging: ELA should predict greater ACC and insula responses to unexpected negative outcomes and smaller ventral striatal and ACC responses to unexpected positive outcomes.

Because the key quantity is the precision-weighted prediction error, not raw activation, the sharpest tests use model-based fMRI to estimate precision and prediction-error signals directly; resting-state data should show the gradient alterations of Section 6.
• Electrophysiology: prediction-error indices (MMN, FRN) should be modulated by ELA history, with enhanced amplitudes to threatening deviants.

The prenatalanxiety findings reviewed in Section 4.2 motivate a sharper, pre-registered prediction: reduced repetition suppression for predictable standards and enhanced responses to threat-related auditory input, tested against non-predictive (attention or arousal) alternatives (Song et al., 2025; Taylor et al., 2024).

text.text: • Individual differences: a measure of precision plasticity (Section 2.5) should moderate the association between early experience and later precision parameters in opposite directions for adverse and supportive environments, a crossover rather than a uniform vulnerability effect.
• Symmetry and supportive input: a "mirror signature" for supportive input would be unfalsifiable, because any inverse of any adversity effect would confirm it, so we specify an asymmetry.

Supportive, structured early environments are predicted to confer faster precision re-tuning when volatility changes: after a contingency reversal, supportively reared individuals should re-normalize learning rates more quickly than both adversity-exposed and average-environment comparisons (Nelson and Gabard-Durnam, 2020).

text.text: The one positive-valence datum in the prenatal literature points the same way: higher maternal mindfulness during pregnancy was associated with smaller infant N250 responses to repeated standards and larger P150 amplitudes, the opposite of the association with maternal anxiety on the same stimuli (van den Heuvel et al., 2015).
A framework that could accommodate every consequence of ELA would not be falsifiable.
We therefore state what this one does not explain and what would count against it.
Primary and secondary domains.
The core domain is threat vigilance and affective learning and decision-making under uncertainty, where precision-like parameters are estimable and the cited evidence is concentrated.
Applications to mood, conduct, and risk-taking (Section 7.1) are secondary and depend on that core.

Processes outside the framework. (i) Effects of biologically proximal insults that act directly on neural tissue or on the plasticity machinery itself (malnutrition, teratogens, hypoxic or preterm brain injury) are predicted to produce general reductions in processing capacity rather than channel-specific biases; recent developmental reviews distinguish these biologically proximal exposures from psychological adversity (Chertoff et al., 2026).

text.text: (ii) Global intellectual impairment after severe deprivation is not a precision bias and is not explained here, although the framework predicts that deprivation-related differences in social and linguistic channels should be dissociable from it. (iii) Somatic outcomes of ELA, such as cardiometabolic disease, are outside the framework except where they feed back on neural computation (Section 7.5).
Observations that would count against the framework.

The core claim would be disconfirmed if ELA-related differences were fully explained by global arousal or attention, without channel specificity; if precision-like parameters showed no association with ELA once baseline expectations (priors) were modeled; if threat, deprivation, and unpredictability produced indistinguishable computational profiles, contrary to
Table 2; or if supportive environments yielded only the inverse of adversity effects without a re-tuning advantage.
7.4 Therapeutic Implications Read through this framework, intervention is recalibration, and the distinction of Section 4.3 determines what should change and how change should be measured.
The proposals below are hypotheses about mechanism, not claims of efficacy.
Exposure-based CBT.

The inhibitory-learning account casts the violation of fearful expectancies as the active ingredient of exposure (Craske et al., 2014); in precision terms, its techniques make disconfirming evidence precise.

text.text: Other approaches.

Real-time fMRI neurofeedback targeting the amygdala has been piloted in combat-related PTSD (Zotev et al., 2018) and could be adapted to train precision-linked ACC or amygdala signals; no ELA-specific trial exists.

text.text: Mindfulness-based training of precision on distressing interoceptive signals is a possibility we note but do not rest any claim on, because it has not been tested as a mechanism in ELA populations.
The framework is stated at the information level.
An energy-level reading is worth developing separately, keeping two levels of description apart.

The first is the energetic cost of neural computation: signaling and wiring are shaped by energetic economy (Attwell and Laughlin, 2001; Bullmore and Sporns, 2012), most of the brain's energy budget is committed to ongoing signaling (Jamadar et al., 2025), and chronic over-precision may be a costly operating point.

text.text: The second is the physiological regulation of energy availability.

The HPA axis is one regulator (Section 2.3); insulin is another, and it also acts as a neuromodulator in the central nervous system, influencing neuronal signaling, synaptic plasticity, and reward-related behavior (Kullmann et al., 2016).

text.text: Insulin signaling therefore offers an experimentally tractable link between early conditions, metabolic regulation, and the reward computations of Section 5.5.
The first testable question is whether metabolic state (e.g., insulin sensitivity) moderates precision and reward-learning parameters in ELA-exposed individuals.

Any energetic extension must also be discriminated from accounts that already formalize cost-constrained inference: the Expected Value of Control theory, which places a costbenefit computation over control signals in the ACC (Shenhav et al., 2013); resourcerational analysis (Lieder and Griffiths, 2020); and an energy-information trade-off derived within predictive coding (Huang et al., 2024).

text.text: Because no biologically serious account assumes unlimited energy, raw metabolic cost or allostatic load would not discriminate an energetic account from a precision-only one; the discriminating evidence would be a specific trade-off in which inferential accuracy is sacrificed to conserve energy under metabolic constraint.

text.text: We have argued that early experience calibrates the developing brain's predictive architecture, and that the most parsimonious and testable locus of that calibration is precision weighting, the gain placed on different classes of prediction error.

Calibration occurs within sensitive periods whose brakes, together with self-confirming sampling of evidence, can stabilize it beyond the conditions that produced it, and susceptibility to it varies between individuals.

Under adversity the system over-weights potential threat and predictable input and under-weights disconfirming evidence; that these biases consolidate into pessimistic priors is a stronger, optional claim, and we have specified the signatures that would distinguish the two.
The ACC is proposed as a hub allocating gain across channels within a distributed circuit whose other nodes make distinct, testable contributions.

The framework states its boundaries, treats supportive input as calibrating the same machinery, and points to interventions aimed not merely at changing beliefs but at recalibrating the processes that weight the evidence for them.
